title: Clinical Indications
subtitle: Where EMDR is supported and where evidence is emerging
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating clinical indications across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain clinical indications in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in clinical indications.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to clinical indications.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR is best established for PTSD and trauma-related symptoms.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Evidence for other conditions is developing but should not be generalised from PTSD without condition-specific trials.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Indication decisions require diagnosis, goals, stability, consent, comorbidity and availability of evidence-based alternatives.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of clinical indications as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need clinical indications to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: “Trauma-informed” does not mean every problem requires trauma processing.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use clinical indications to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses clinical indications to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: “Trauma-informed” does not mean every problem requires trauma processing. Evidence classification: established for PTSD; emerging elsewhere.
